opening.headline: This explains the reasons why an observability agent in a Kubernetes environment misses some pods, based on the behavior of the Cluster Agent and Autodiscovery.
body: In environments where pods constantly come and go, humans cannot manage a list of collection targets. Therefore, container observation is achieved through annotations attached to pods, and some pods are omitted when annotations are inconsistent.

This course examines the role delegation between Cluster Agent and Node Agent, the process by which configurations are applied via Autodiscovery, and the requirements for APM activation. It also explains how to identify root causes by analyzing annotation errors and their scope of symptoms.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the operation of Cluster Agent and Autodiscovery.
The causes of observation omission can be distinguished in the collection setup.

screens.title: Some pods are not observable in Kubernetes
screens.lead: First, let's examine the situation where observations are missing in a Kubernetes environment. Review the scene to confirm how omissions are represented.

paragraphs: There are six pods running in the cluster, but only four are displayed on the observation screen. For the same service, some pods have both metrics and traces, while others are empty.

Pods constantly appear and disappear based on deployment, scaling, and failure recovery. The previous approach of installing an agent on a single server and maintaining a list of targets is no longer feasible to keep up with these changes. At the moment when a person manages the list of collection targets, omissions inevitably occur.

Therefore, observation in container environments is declared rather than listed. Labels and annotations attached to pods indicate what should be collected, and the agent begins collecting data upon pod startup by reading the declaration.
In this class, we will describe the operation of the Cluster Agent and Autodiscovery, and distinguish the causes of observation gaps based on collection configurations.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Can we determine where to suspect merely from the fact that a missing pod is only a part of the whole? Try to answer this question by the end of the class.

visual.alt: A cluster diagram showing four pods observed and two missing due to different reasons out of six pods.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how data collection takes place in a container environment.

screens.title: Can you explain the observability data collection approach in container environments?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about the answer on your own before clicking it.

items.prompt: What's the difference between installing an agent on a single server and operating in an environment where pods continuously change?
items.answer: In a server environment, the target rarely changes, so once settings are configured, they can remain unchanged. In a pod environment, the target continuously changes, so the settings must be attached to and follow the target. Therefore, the pod's own declaration becomes the basis for collection settings.

items.prompt: Who informs me about the collection settings of a new pod when it is created?
items.answer: Annotations, labels, or agent configuration templates attached to a pod are provided. When a container starts, the agent automatically finds and applies the matching template. This functionality is called Autodiscovery.

items.prompt: Where do I get the cluster-wide information and node-specific information from?
items.answer: Cluster-level metadata is available only to the API server, while node-level metrics are read by the kubelet on each node. If all agents directly query both sources, the load would become excessive, hence a role separation structure is required.

screens.outro: Based on the raised questions, we will begin by examining the role allocation of agents.

screens.title: Role delegation between Cluster Agent and Node Agent
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to proceed step by step through the structure where data flows from the node, through the Cluster Agent, to the API server.

steps.title: Node Agent
steps.body: The Node Agent runs on each node. By narrowing its role to only handle metrics read by kubelet and node-level metadata, the number of RBAC rules required for the agent is reduced. The lower the privileges, the lower the risk if compromised.

steps.title: Cluster Agent
steps.body: The Cluster Agent acts as a proxy between the API server and node Agents. Since all node Agents do not need to directly query the API server, the load on the API server is reduced.

steps.title: Metadata transmission
steps.body: The Cluster Agent delivers cluster-level metadata to the Node Agent, which is available only on the API server. The Node Agent attaches this metadata to metrics, enabling richer information collection. For example, it includes information such as the deployment name to which a pod belongs.

steps.title: Cluster-level features
steps.body: The cluster-level functions such as service level monitoring, event collection, and HPA based on external metrics are handled by the Cluster Agent. This consolidates tasks that must not be performed redundantly across nodes into a single location.

steps.title: Basic activation
steps.body: If Helm charts version 2.7.0 or later, or Datadog Operator version 1.0.0 or later, are installed, the Cluster Agent is enabled by default. If you install using a custom manifest, you must verify that the Cluster Agent is enabled. In this architecture, the Node Agent does not directly connect to the API server but instead receives metadata through the Cluster Agent; therefore, if the Cluster Agent is disabled, rich tags may appear empty.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the role, let's now examine the code for Pod-level Autodiscovery that is configured through code.

screens.title: Autodiscovery: The process of applying configurations to a container
screens.lead: Read the following deployment snippet from top to bottom, and verify the meaning of each line against the right-side description to check for mismatches.

notes.note: In objects that indirectly define pods, such as deployments, annotations should be placed under spec.template.metadata. If annotations are placed at the top-level metadata, they will not be attached to the pod, causing the autodiscovery mechanism to fail reading those settings and resulting in missing integrated metrics.
The cache in the middle of the key is the container name. It must exactly match the name in the containers section. If the names do not match, the template will not be applied.

This is a JSON that specifies which integration to enable with which instance configuration. Using %%host%% in the value will be replaced with the pod IP. The configuration cannot be read if the JSON syntax is incorrect.
If the container's name is not cache but redis, the key and name do not match, resulting in symptoms showing only the integrated metric. Other metrics remain normal, making detection delayed.

Autodiscovery finds and automatically applies a matching integrated configuration template when a container starts. Configuration can be declared using pod annotations, files, ConfigMap, or key-value stores. In the file format, the template is applied when ad_identifiers match the container image name.

screens.outro: Having read about autodiscovery, let's compare the requirements for integrating with APM.

screens.title: APM Activation and Integrated Configuration
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the settings required by the APM agent and app pods for APM to function.

tabs.label: agent
tabs.body: APM requires activation on the agent side and configuration on the app pod side. On the agent side, for Operator, set `features.apm.enabled` to true, and for Helm, set `datadog.apm.socketEnabled` to enable the UDS socket. The agent must be in a state where it can receive traces.

tabs.label: App Pod
tabs.body: The app pod mounts socket volume or has the Admission Controller inject environment variables and volumes to send traces to the agent. Traces will not arrive if the agent is enabled alone and there are no pod-side configurations. Injection occurs when the pod is created, so it may not apply to already-running pods.

tabs.label: Transmission method
tabs.body: The trace transmission methods are UDS, TCP (IP and port), and Kubernetes service, with UDS being recommended. The method must be consistent between the agent and the app pod; if only one side is changed, traces will not arrive. UDS uses a shared socket file approach, making it less dependent on network configurations, whereas TCP or service methods require proper matching of port and name resolution.

tabs.label: Exception Integration
tabs.body: Some integrations, such as Ceph and Varnish, cannot be used with Autodiscovery due to requirements for process trees or filesystem access. Not all integrations work solely through annotations, so compatibility with Autodiscovery must be verified for each integration. Integrations that are not compatible require a separate setup method at the host level, in which case changing pod annotations will not result in metrics being collected. If the symptoms are limited to integration metrics, first verify compatibility with the integration.

screens.outro: I have organized the configuration requirements; now I will explain cases where annotations are inconsistent.

screens.title: Explanation example: Annotation is missing, so autodiscovery does not work.
screens.lead: The instructor explains a case where only some of the pods deployed with the same image have empty integration metrics. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Case conditions
steps.body: Among pods deployed from the same image, only pods created in a new deployment have empty integration metrics. The instructor reads the YAML files side by side for normal pods and missing pods to identify the differences.

steps.title: Step 1: Normal Pod
steps.body: The normal pod has the `ad.datadoghq.com/cache.checks` annotation in the pod's metadata, and the container name is cached. Since the key name matches the container name, the template is applied.

steps.title: Step 2: Location Error
steps.body: The deployment of a missing pod did not have the same annotation attached to the pod, instead it should be moved below `spec.template.metadata`. The deployment location is easily confused.

steps.title: Step 3: Name Mismatch
steps.body: Another pod changed the container name to redis, but the key remains cache, so they do not match. The key name should be updated to match the containers' name. A rule is needed to also update the annotation key when changing the container name.

steps.title: Step 4: Review after modification
steps.body: After the new pod is created, the settings are automatically applied. Existing pods require a redeployment. After application, directly verify that integrated metrics are being received. If any metric is missing, repeat the inspection. First verify on a single modified pod, and if no issues are found, apply the changes to the entire deployment.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: The root cause of this case was not the agent but the pod specification. Two conditions—annotation location and annotation key containing the container name—were required for the Autodiscovery operation, and ensuring these conditions were met must be managed within the deployment template. Manually modifying YAML files individually leads to repeated errors, so it is better to use a common template for the annotation block.

screens.outro: The cause might not be a single one; therefore, we will look at methods for distinguishing between causes on the agent side and the app side.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Differentiating Agent-Side Causes from App-Side Causes
screens.lead: When you select a symptom, the suspected location and verification items will be displayed. First, think about where you'd like to view, then click.

items.prompt: Symptom 1: No traces are available from any pods.
items.answer: First suspect the APM activation or socket configuration on the agent side. If everything is empty, the agent's configuration—common to all—might be the root cause. Check whether APM is activated and whether the socket is open. If the transmission method was recently changed, verify that both the agent and application sides are using the same method. If a single configuration change affected all pods simultaneously, the issue is more likely on the agent side.

items.prompt: Symptom 2: Traces are missing from some pods only.
items.answer: Suspect the socket mount or injection configuration of this pod. Check whether the pod was created before the injection functionality was enabled. If only some elements are missing, different components may be responsible for each pod. Verify whether the pod was created before injection occurred or whether the socket volume was mounted. By placing a normal pod and a missing pod side by side and comparing their environment variables and volume lists, the differences will become immediately apparent.

Verify that the annotation key matches the container name and that the annotation exists in the pod metadata. Also check whether the integration is compatible with Autodiscovery. Other metrics are normal, so the agent itself is likely not the issue. Since this symptom is discovered latest, it's advisable to have separate alerts for integration metrics being missing.

items.prompt: The first question we should ask is: what?
items.answer: Whether the scope is complete or partial is the first clue regarding agent configuration and pod configuration. If the scope is complete, start with the agent configuration; if partial, begin with the pod configuration. This distinction helps save time. Without making this distinction and instead starting with agent logs, you may miss different root causes across pods. Confirming the scope takes only a few minutes and should always be your first step.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizes the core of the lesson in one go.

paragraphs: Observation in container environments is declarative rather than imperative. Pod labels and annotations serve as the basis for collection configurations, and Autodiscovery automatically applies configurations that match container names or images.

The Cluster Agent handles cluster-level information forwarding, while the Node Agent is responsible for node-level data collection. APM requires configuration on both the agents and the application pods.

Once you answer the initial question, the fact that only some pods are missing serves as a clue to suspect the pod-side declaration first. If all pods are empty, check the agent; if only some are empty, verify the pod annotations or socket settings.

In practice, follow these three habits: when deploying a new service, include annotations in a common template; when changing a container name, update the corresponding key as well; and when a missing item is detected, first verify the scope. By adhering to these three practices, most container observability gaps can be prevented before deployment.

glossary.def: An agent that relays cluster-level data and metadata between the API server and node Agent.
This is a feature that automatically finds and applies the matching integrated configuration template when a container starts.
This is configuration for per-environment checks and logs declared via annotations or files.
Enabling both agent trace reception and app pod transmission settings simultaneously.
List of container image names to apply templates from file-based settings.

misconceptions.myth: Once the agent is installed, all pods are automatically collected.
misconceptions.fact: Integrated settings must match the container, and APM also requires pod-level configurations.

misconceptions.myth: The container name for the annotation can be anything.
misconceptions.fact: The container name specified in the key must match the name in spec.containers.
Process trees or certain integrations requiring file access cannot be achieved using Autodiscovery.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: The Cluster Agent handles collection at the cluster level, while the Node Agent handles collection at the node level.
Autodiscovery automatically applies configurations that match container names or images.
Whether the scope of omission is complete or partial determines the agent and pod configuration.
closing.reflectionLead: The following question is for your own reflection. Answers will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: When a new pod is created in our cluster, how is the collection configuration applied via a declaration, and how can we verify whether it has been applied?

checks.q: There is an annotation named ad.datadoghq.com/cache.checks in the spec.template.metadata of the deployment, and the container name is redis. What happens in this case?
options: The container name is different, so the integrated configuration is not applied.
Since it has an annotation, it is automatically matched and applied by image name.
The key cache is interpreted and applied based on the pod name.
The node Agent converts the container name to a cache.
checks.explain: Among the annotation keys, the middle part is the container name and must match the name in containers; otherwise, only integration metrics are exposed, and symptoms arise.

wrong.1: Image name matching uses the file-based ad_identifiers method, and the annotation key uses the container name.
wrong.2: The key portion refers to the container name, not the pod name.
wrong.3: The agent does not change the container name.

checks.intro: You've just learned about the relationship between annotations and container names. Select the result when the names mismatch. This is an unrecorded self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The template will not be applied if the container name of the key does not match.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Consider what the name inside the annotation key should be for the setting to apply.

checks.q: Pair up the components with their roles.
right: One per node, managing kubelet metrics
Inject tracing environment variables and volumes into the app pod
Acts as a proxy between the API server and node Agent, forwarding cluster-level information
Apply the matching integrated settings template automatically when the container starts.
checks.explain: The Cluster Agent reduces API server load and provides cluster information, while the Node Agent handles node-level data collection. Autodiscovery automatically applies configuration templates, and the Admission Controller injects app pod configurations.
checks.intro: Pair up the components with their roles. Scores are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Connected all components and roles appropriately.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There's a mismatch somewhere. At the cluster level, node level, configuration application, and environment variable injection—determine who is responsible for each.

checks.q: Tracing is missing not from all pods, but only from some pods. Where should we start investigating?
options: Helm chart version for the entire cluster
Cluster Agent's external metric HPA functionality
This pod's socket mount or injection settings
checks.explain: Whether it's scoped to the entire system or just a part is the first clue provided by agent and pod configurations. If only certain pods are affected, it first examines the socket mounts or injection settings of those specific pods.

wrong.0: If there's an issue with the agent, there will be no traces across all pods.
wrong.1: Chart version is an element applied uniformly across the entire cluster.
wrong.2: HPA has no relation to trace collection.

checks.intro: Consider the initial inspection point for situations where tracing is missing in some pods. This is an unrecorded self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. If only some of them are empty, then the socket mounting or injection settings of the corresponding pod should be suspected initially.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Review the scope again. By looking for the issue in common settings across the entire system rather than just in some pods, you move away from the root cause.
